rw: Living within your means means keeping spending at or below your income each month, so you avoid debt and can still build savings for the future.

ww.Spending more than you make: Spending more than you make is living beyond your means, which forces you to use debt or savings and is the opposite of the idea.
ww.Never spending money on anything: Never spending anything is unrealistic because everyone must pay for needs like food and housing; living within your means only requires spending to fit your income.
ww.Borrowing money for every purchase: Borrowing for every purchase means spending beyond current income and piling up debt, which is the opposite of living within your means.

rw: Delayed gratification means giving up an immediate purchase to get something better later, and saving for months toward a quality item is a classic example of it.

ww.Spending your whole paycheck on the same: Spending an entire paycheck right away is the opposite of delayed gratification, since it gives up any chance to save or plan for bigger goals.
ww.Buying the first item you see in a store: Buying the first item you see on a whim is impulse buying, which is immediate gratification rather than waiting for something better or planned.
ww.Charging a purchase you cannot repay to: Charging a purchase you cannot repay is immediate gratification paid for with debt and interest, so it is the reverse of waiting and saving first.

rw: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative you give up, so spending the $100 on tickets means losing $100 of progress toward the needed laptop.

ww.Nothing, because tickets are a want, so: Tickets being a want does not make them free; the $100 spent could have gone toward the laptop, so something valuable is still given up.
ww.The price of the laptop plus sales tax a: The laptop's price plus tax and delivery is the cost of buying the laptop, not what is given up by choosing the tickets instead.
ww.The cost of parking at the big concert v: Parking is an extra out-of-pocket expense of attending the concert, not the opportunity cost, which is the best alternative use of the $100.

rw: FDIC insurance protects deposits up to $250,000 per depositor per bank if the bank fails, whereas cash at home can be stolen or burned with no protection.

ww.Cash kept at home earns higher interest: Cash kept at home earns no interest at all, while a savings account pays interest, so this claim reverses the real difference between them.
ww.Savings accounts cannot be used when an: Savings accounts can be accessed in an emergency, usually by transfer or withdrawal, so this does not explain why they are safer than home cash.
ww.Banks never charge any fees on a savings: Banks can charge fees on savings accounts, such as monthly maintenance or excess withdrawal fees, so the word never makes this statement false.

rw: Interest is the money a bank pays you for letting it use your deposits, usually stated as an annual rate, and it grows your balance over time.

ww.Interest is the amount you deposit every: Money you put into the account is a deposit; interest is instead the amount the bank pays you for using your money, not what you contribute.
ww.Interest is a fee you pay for opening an: Interest is not an account opening fee; fees are charges you pay, while savings interest is a payment made to you by the bank.
ww.Interest is a tax you owe to the governm: Interest earned on savings is not a tax, although it may be taxable income; it is a payment from the bank, not an amount owed to government.

rw: Compound interest: $2,000 x 1.03 x 1.03 = $2,121.80, which rounds to about $2,122 because interest in year two also earns interest.

ww.About $2,060: This adds only simple interest for one year ($2,000 x 3% = $60) and ignores the second year, so it is far too low.
ww.About $2,180: This option was reworded so it is clearly wrong; the correct total is $2,000 x 1.03 x 1.03 = $2,121.80, and $2,180 would need a higher rate.
ww.About $2,600: About $2,600 would require roughly 30 percent growth, far above the 3% annual rate; $2,000 x 1.03^2 is only about $2,122.

rw: Separating goal savings from a small fun budget keeps savings untouched and gives you guilt-free spending money, which helps you resist raiding savings for small wants.

ww.Carry large amounts of cash with you eve: Carrying large amounts of cash makes spending easier and risks loss or theft, so it makes dipping into savings for wants more likely, not less.
ww.Keep all of your money in one single acc: Keeping everything in one account with no tracking or limits blurs savings and spending money, which makes it easy to spend savings on small wants.
ww.Cancel your savings account and spend wh: Closing your savings account and spending the money is the exact opposite of protecting savings and would leave you with nothing for goals or emergencies.

rw: FDIC insurance covers deposits in insured banks up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category, and pays out if the bank fails.

ww.Cash that is kept in a safe at home for: FDIC insurance does not cover cash kept at home; it only protects money deposited in FDIC-insured banks, so home cash has no such protection.
ww.Stocks that are bought through a bank or: Stocks bought through a bank or broker are investments, not deposits, so FDIC insurance does not cover them; SIPC covers broker failure, not losses.
ww.Losses that are caused by a drop in the: FDIC insurance does not protect against market losses on investments; it only guarantees bank deposits if the bank itself fails, not falling stock prices.

rw: Closing an old card shortens your average account age and removes available credit, which can raise your utilization ratio, and both effects may lower your score.

ww.Old accounts are not counted in any cred: Old accounts do count in credit scores; length of credit history is a scoring factor, which is why closing them can matter at all.
ww.Closed accounts are always deleted at on: Closed accounts in good standing often stay on your report for about ten years, so they are not deleted at once and the score drop has other causes.
ww.Banks punish customers for canceling the: Banks do not punish customers for closing cards; the score may fall because of changed history length and utilization, which are mathematical effects.

rw: A 780 score signals reliable repayment, so lenders see less default risk and generally offer a lower interest rate on the $15,000 car loan.

ww.Neither of them can get a loan from any: Lenders do approve loans for fair or good credit scores, usually at higher rates for lower scores, so neither being denied outright is a safe assumption.
ww.Both will receive exactly the same rate: Lenders price loans based on risk, so different credit scores lead to different rates; the same rate for both borrowers is unlikely.
ww.The person with the 620 score, because l: A 620 score signals higher default risk, so lenders charge more interest to offset that risk rather than offering a cheaper rate.

rw: A variable rate is tied to a benchmark such as the prime rate, so it can rise or fall over time and change your payment amount.

ww.A rate that is chosen by the borrower at: A borrower does not choose the rate; the lender sets it, and the term variable means the rate can change over time, not that it is picked by the borrower.
ww.A rate that is always set at zero for th: A rate fixed at zero would be an interest-free loan, which is rare; a variable rate instead moves with market conditions above zero.
ww.A rate that never changes during the who: A rate that never changes during the loan is a fixed rate, which is the opposite of a variable rate that adjusts with the market.

rw: A fixed interest rate stays the same for the whole loan term, so the rate and usually the payment are predictable and do not change with the market.

ww.A rate that is repaid at the end of the: Fixed refers to the rate staying constant, not to repaying everything at the end; most loans charge interest along the way, not only at maturity.
ww.A rate that is free of charge for the bo: Interest is the price of borrowing and is not free; a fixed rate is still charged, it just does not change over the loan.
ww.A rate that changes each month with the: A rate that changes monthly with the market is a variable rate, which is the opposite of a fixed rate that stays constant.

rw: APR combines the interest rate and certain fees into one yearly percentage, so it is the best way to compare the true cost of loans from different lenders.

ww.The color of the loan paperwork: The color of the paperwork says nothing about borrowing costs; the cost is shown in the interest rate and fees, which APR combines into one yearly percentage.
ww.The number of branches lenders have: The number of branches tells you about convenience, not what the loan costs; it cannot be used to compare the yearly price of borrowing.
ww.The size of the lender's building: The lender's building size has no link to loan pricing; APR is the standardized measure that lets you compare real borrowing costs across lenders.

rw: A major change like buying a house raises the value you need to protect and adds new risks, so reviewing coverage keeps you from being underinsured.

ww.Insurance is only needed once in a lifet: Insurance needs change with life events, so it is not a once-in-a-lifetime purchase; major changes like a home purchase require updating your coverage.
ww.Insurance policies update themselves for: Policies do not update themselves automatically at no charge; you must contact the insurer to change coverage, and higher coverage usually raises the premium.
ww.Reviewing a policy cancels it and ends y: Reviewing a policy does not cancel it; you simply check whether limits and coverage still fit, and the policy remains in force during the review.

rw: State minimum limits are often low, so a serious injury claim can exceed them, and the at-fault driver may have to pay the excess out of pocket.

ww.The other driver must pay for everything: The other driver is not responsible for your costs; as the at-fault driver you owe damages, and the issue is limits being too low to cover them.
ww.No costs will be owed because it was an: Causing an accident accidentally still creates liability, since negligence rather than intent determines responsibility, so costs can definitely be owed.
ww.The insurer will pay unlimited amounts n: Liability policies pay only up to their stated limits, so the insurer will not pay unlimited amounts and the driver must cover anything above them.

rw: Working smoke detectors give early warning and avoiding overloaded outlets prevents electrical fires, so together these actions lower the chance and damage of a home fire.

ww.Leaving candles burning while you sleep: Leaving candles burning unattended while you sleep is a common cause of house fires, so it raises fire risk rather than reducing it.
ww.Removing the batteries from all of the s: Removing smoke detector batteries disables the early warning that saves lives, so it increases the danger of a fire rather than reducing it.
ww.Storing flammable liquids close to a hea: Storing flammable liquids near a heater or gas stove invites ignition and fire, so it raises the risk of a home fire.

rw: Self-insurance means setting aside your own money to cover possible losses instead of buying a policy, and it works best for small, predictable risks.

ww.Asking a friend to promise to pay for a: A friend's promise to pay is an informal arrangement and not self-insurance, which means setting aside your own funds to absorb losses yourself.
ww.Ignoring the possibility of loss and hop: Ignoring risk and hoping for the best is risk acceptance without any plan, not self-insurance, which involves actually saving funds to pay for losses.
ww.Buying a policy from an insurance compan: Buying a yearly policy from an insurance company transfers risk to the insurer, so it is traditional insurance, the opposite of self-insuring.

rw: Insurance fits rare but very costly events like a house fire or major illness, which would wipe out savings, so spreading risk across many policyholders makes sense.

ww.A regular expense that comes up every mo: Regular predictable expenses such as rent or food are budgeted for, not insured, since insurance covers uncertain losses and not certain recurring bills.
ww.A cost that you choose to avoid complete: Completely avoiding a cost is risk avoidance, a different strategy from insurance, which covers risks you are still exposed to.
ww.A small cost that you can easily pay fro: A small cost you can easily afford is better handled by saving and self-insuring, since insurance premiums would likely cost more than the loss.

rw: Liquid means you can sell the asset quickly for cash without losing much value, like savings or shares of large companies.

ww.It never changes in value over time at a: A liquid investment is easy to convert to cash, which has nothing to do with value staying fixed; liquid assets can still rise and fall in price.
ww.It cannot be sold for several years in a: An asset that cannot be sold for years is illiquid, which is the opposite of liquid; liquidity is about how quickly you can turn it into cash.
ww.It is stored as water or some other flui: Liquid here is a financial term, not a physical state of matter; the word describes how easily an asset converts to cash, not its form.

rw: Cash in checking is already money and can be used immediately, so it is the most liquid asset on the list.

ww.A house in a nice neighborhood: A house takes weeks or months to sell and has closing costs, so it is illiquid compared with cash in a checking account.
ww.A rare painting from a gallery: A rare painting needs a specialized buyer and appraisal, which makes selling slow and uncertain, so it is far less liquid than cash.
ww.A piece of land in the country: Land can take a long time to sell and its value depends on location and buyers, so it is illiquid compared with cash.

rw: Diversification means spreading money across many investments so one failure does not ruin you; putting everything into one company's stock ignores it.

ww.Tax deferral: Tax deferral delays taxes on investment growth; it has nothing to do with losing everything when a single company fails, which is concentration risk.
ww.Compounding: Compounding is earning returns on prior returns, which does not address the danger of holding only one company's stock that can fail.
ww.Inflation cover: Inflation cover is not a standard investing principle; the risk of loss from a single failed company is controlled by diversification instead.

rw: A stock market index, such as the S&P 500 or Dow, measures the performance of a chosen group of stocks and shows how the market is doing.

ww.A single company's yearly profit report: A company's yearly profit report is an income statement, which describes one firm, while an index tracks the performance of many stocks together.
ww.A government rule about taxes on stock t: Tax rules on stock trades come from government law, such as capital gains tax, and are not what an index is, which only measures performance.
ww.A list of the fees that brokers charge c: A list of broker fees is a fee schedule, not an index; an index tracks stock prices and gives a snapshot of market performance.

rw: Rebalancing means buying or selling to restore your target mix of assets, such as 60% stocks and 40% bonds, which keeps your risk level on plan.

ww.Selling everything and starting over fro: Selling everything and starting over each year is expensive because of taxes and trading costs; rebalancing only adjusts holdings back to targets.
ww.Buying only the single best performer in: Buying only the best performer concentrates risk and abandons the target mix, which is the opposite of rebalancing a diversified portfolio.
ww.Ignoring the portfolio for years on end: Ignoring a portfolio lets asset weights drift away from your plan, so it is the opposite of rebalancing, which restores the intended mix.

rw: Long-term investors generally do best staying with their plan and continuing regular investing, which buys more shares at lower prices during a dip.

ww.Borrow money so you can buy a single sto: Borrowing to buy a single stock adds debt and concentration risk during a downturn, which is a risky response rather than a sensible one.
ww.Sell everything immediately because of f: Selling everything out of fear locks in losses and often misses the recovery, which makes it a poor response for a long-term investor.
ww.Stop looking at the plan and give up on: Abandoning the plan and giving up on your goal turns a temporary decline into a permanent setback, which is not a sensible response.

rw: The saying advises diversification, spreading money across different investments so that one loss does not destroy your whole portfolio.

ww.Spend all of your money on eggs and bask: This takes the saying literally; the proverb is about diversifying risk, and spending all your money on eggs and baskets has nothing to do with investing.
ww.Buy only one single stock that you trust: Buying one stock puts all your eggs in one basket, which is exactly what the saying warns against because one failure can wipe you out.
ww.Avoid investing in anything at all, ever: Avoiding investing altogether misses the lesson; the saying advises spreading money around, not refusing to invest, and cash can lose value to inflation.

rw: A 401(k) match is extra money your employer adds to your account based on what you contribute, which is a free boost to retirement savings.

ww.It guarantees investment gains every sin: A match adds money but guarantees no investment gains; the account's investments can still lose value, so returns are never guaranteed.
ww.It lets you withdraw money any time with: Withdrawals from a 401(k) before age 59 and a half usually bring taxes and a 10 percent penalty, so the match does not allow free access.
ww.It lowers your income tax to zero every: Traditional 401(k) contributions reduce taxable income but do not lower taxes to zero, and the match itself has no such effect.

rw: Over 30 years the higher 7% return compounds much more strongly than 4%, so that investor ends with far more money for the same deposits.

ww.Neither investor earns any growth at all: Both investors earn growth because 4% and 7% are both positive returns; saying neither earns growth ignores the compounding that happens each year.
ww.The 4% investor ends up with the larger: The 4% investor earns a lower return on identical deposits, so ends with a smaller balance, not a larger one.
ww.Both investors end up with the same fina: Different returns over 30 years produce very different balances because compounding magnifies the gap, so the final amounts cannot be the same.

rw: A bear market is a sustained decline in stock prices, commonly defined as a fall of 20 percent or more from a recent high.

ww.A period when prices rise steadily over: Steadily rising prices describe a bull market, not a bear market, which is the opposite condition of falling prices.
ww.A period when stock markets close for a: Stock markets closing for a holiday is just a normal break in trading and has nothing to do with a bear market, which is about falling prices.
ww.A market where people buy and sell wild: A bear market is a financial term about stock prices and has nothing to do with trading animals; the name refers to a bear swiping downward.

rw: A bull market is a period of rising or expected rising stock prices, with investor optimism, and the name comes from a bull thrusting its horns upward.

ww.A period when prices fall sharply and in: Sharp falling prices and investor fear describe a bear market, which is the opposite of a bull market.
ww.A market where only livestock is traded: A bull market refers to rising security prices, not a livestock market; the word is a financial term unrelated to trading cattle.
ww.A period when prices never change at all: Prices never changing for many years would be a flat or stagnant market, not a bull market, which is defined by rising prices.

rw: In a stock split, a company issues more shares and lowers the price per share proportionally, so each holder's total value stays the same.

ww.A company gives half its yearly profits: Sharing half of profits with staff is profit sharing, not a stock split, which only changes the number of shares and not company earnings.
ww.A company merges with one of its rivals: Merging with a rival is a merger or acquisition, which combines companies; a stock split only divides existing shares into more pieces.
ww.A company cuts its workforce in half to: Cutting the workforce in half is a layoff or restructuring and is unrelated to a stock split, which changes only the number of shares.

rw: Past performance does not guarantee future results, which is why investment ads carry this warning; markets change and previous gains may not repeat.

ww.It guarantees the same results next year: Past performance cannot guarantee next year's results, since markets change, so saying it guarantees the same outcome is false.
ww.It is the only factor that matters: Past performance is only one piece of information; costs, risk, goals and economic conditions matter too, so it is not the only factor.
ww.It proves an investment cannot lose cash: A good track record does not prove an investment cannot lose money; every investment carries risk, even one that has done well in the past.

rw: A diversified mix of investments that has outpaced inflation helps long-term savings keep or grow their purchasing power over decades.

ww.Spending all of your savings right away: Spending all your savings right away gives up future purchasing power altogether and does nothing to protect it from inflation.
ww.Keeping all of your savings in cash for: Cash earning little interest loses buying power to inflation over decades, so holding all savings in cash does not protect them.
ww.Hiding cash in a drawer at home for deca: Cash in a drawer earns no interest, so inflation steadily reduces what it can buy, and it also risks loss or theft.

rw: Tracking a month of spending shows exactly where money goes, which reveals patterns and gives a base for budgeting and cutting waste.

ww.Stop looking at your account balance for: Not checking your balance hides spending problems and may cause overdrafts, so it does not help you gain control over your spending.
ww.Cancel your bank account altogether and: Cancelling your bank account and using only cash removes safety and records and does not itself show where your money goes.
ww.Borrow money so you can cover your purch: Borrowing to cover purchases adds debt and interest, which makes spending harder to control rather than easier.

rw: Paying the full statement balance by the due date keeps the grace period, so purchases are not charged interest at all.

ww.Use the card only for cash advances at t: Cash advances usually carry fees and start accruing interest immediately with no grace period, so they increase interest costs rather than avoid them.
ww.Pay the bill a few days after the due da: Paying after the due date usually triggers a late fee and may lose the grace period, so interest and penalties apply.
ww.Pay only the minimum amount each month o: Paying only the minimum leaves a balance that accrues interest, which can make the debt costly and slow to pay off.

rw: A cash advance is borrowing cash against your card, usually at a higher rate, with an upfront fee and interest from day one.

ww.Earning cash back on the purchases you m: Earning cash back is a rewards benefit for purchases, not a cash advance, which is borrowing actual cash against your credit line.
ww.Paying a bill early using your own money: Paying a bill early from savings uses your own money and involves no card borrowing, so it is not a cash advance.
ww.Depositing cash into your own bank accou: Depositing cash into your own account is a normal bank deposit, not a card transaction, so it has nothing to do with cash advances.

rw: Earned income comes from work such as wages and salary, while unearned income comes from sources like interest, dividends and rent without working.

ww.Earned income comes from gifts; unearned: This reverses the definitions; earned income comes from working at jobs and pay, while gifts are not earned income.
ww.Earned income is never taxed, unearned a: Earned income is taxed, including income tax and payroll taxes, and unearned income such as interest is also generally taxable, so the claim is wrong.
ww.There is no real difference between the: There is a real difference: earned income comes from working, unearned income comes from assets, and they are taxed differently in many cases.

rw: An emergency fund covers unplanned costs like medical bills or car repairs so you do not need credit cards or loans that would add interest.

ww.It is meant for planned vacations and tr: Planned vacations belong in a separate savings goal, since an emergency fund should be reserved for unexpected, urgent expenses.
ww.It is meant to grow quickly through risk: An emergency fund should be safe and easy to access, not exposed to risky bets that could lose value when you need it.
ww.It replaces the need for insurance of al: An emergency fund cannot replace insurance because one major accident or illness can cost far more than the fund holds.

rw: Income is money received from work, investments, or other sources such as interest, gifts or benefits, and it funds spending and saving.

ww.Money a person spends on needs and wants: Money spent on needs and wants is expenses, which is the opposite of income, the money coming in.
ww.Money borrowed from a bank for a large p: Money borrowed from a bank is a loan that must be repaid, not income, which does not create an obligation to repay.
ww.Money set aside for use in an emergency: Money set aside for emergencies is savings, which is held from income already received rather than being the income itself.

rw: Wages are paid by the hour worked, so pay varies with hours, while a salary is a fixed yearly amount split across pay periods.

ww.There is no difference between the two t: There is a difference: wages are paid by the hour, while salaried workers get a fixed amount per year regardless of hours.
ww.Wages are fixed yearly pay; a salary is: This reverses the definitions; wages are hourly pay and salary is a fixed yearly amount, not the other way around.
ww.Wages are tips; a salary is a bonus paid: Tips and bonuses are separate types of compensation, so equating wages with tips and salary with bonuses is incorrect.

rw: Gross pay is the hourly rate times hours worked, so $18 x 25 = $450 per week before taxes and deductions.

ww.$43: $43 is $18 plus $25 added together; gross pay uses multiplication, so the correct figure is $18 x 25 = $450.
ww.$4,500: $4,500 is ten times too large, likely from a misplaced decimal; $18 x 25 hours equals $450, not $4,500.
ww.$225: $225 is half of the correct amount, as if only 12.5 hours were counted; $18 x 25 hours equals $450.

rw: Regular pay is 40 x $15 = $600, overtime is 6 x $22.50 = $135, and the total is $735.

ww.$1,035: $1,035 pays all 46 hours at 1.5 times rate; overtime applies only to hours past 40, so the correct total is $735.
ww.$690: $690 is 46 hours at the regular $15 rate with no overtime premium; the 6 overtime hours should be paid at $22.50.
ww.$600: $600 counts only the first 40 hours and leaves out the 6 overtime hours; adding 6 x $22.50 = $135 gives $735.

rw: Federal income tax withholding is required by law, and employers must deduct it from each paycheck based on the worker's W-4.

ww.A gym fee the worker chose to pay: A gym fee chosen by the worker is a voluntary deduction; the law does not require it, unlike taxes withheld by an employer.
ww.A parking space fee at the office: A parking fee is an optional arrangement with the employer and not a legal requirement, so it is a voluntary deduction.
ww.A charity donation made at work: A charity donation made at work is voluntary, so it is a chosen deduction, not one required by law like taxes.

rw: FICA taxes fund Social Security, which pays retirement and disability benefits, and Medicare, which provides health coverage for seniors and some others.

ww.Public schools and libraries: Public schools and libraries are mostly funded by local property taxes and state revenue, not by FICA payroll taxes.
ww.Public highways and bridges: Highways and bridges are funded mainly by fuel taxes and government budgets, not by FICA, which supports Social Security and Medicare.
ww.National parks and forests: National parks and forests are paid for through federal budgets and fees, not through FICA payroll taxes meant for Social Security and Medicare.

rw: Multiply gross pay by the FICA rate: $2,000 x 0.0765 = $153 withheld for Social Security and Medicare.

ww.$15.30: $15.30 is moved one decimal place too small; 7.65% of $2,000 is $153, not $15.30.
ww.$765: $765 is 38 percent of $2,000 and uses the wrong rate; 7.65% x $2,000 = $153.
ww.$1,530: $1,530 is ten times too much, from a decimal error; 0.0765 x $2,000 = $153.

rw: Take-home pay, or net pay, is what remains after taxes and deductions are subtracted from your gross pay.

ww.Pay from tips and bonuses only: Pay from tips and bonuses only is a partial description of earnings and does not describe take-home pay, which is what remains after deductions.
ww.Pay for overtime hours only: Overtime pay is extra pay for hours past 40, and it is not the same as take-home pay, which is after deductions.
ww.Pay before any deductions at all: Pay before any deductions is gross pay, which is the opposite of take-home pay, also called net pay.

rw: The W-4 tells your employer how much federal income tax to withhold from your paycheck based on your filing status and allowances.

ww.A form reporting yearly wages and the ta: A form reporting yearly wages and taxes paid to date is the W-2, which the employer gives the worker after the year, not the W-4.
ww.A form for requesting vacation time from: A vacation request is an internal company form and has nothing to do with taxes, which the W-4 handles.
ww.A form for applying to a job at a local: A job application is filled out when applying; the W-4 is completed after hiring to set tax withholding.

rw: An independent contractor is self-employed, chooses how the work is done, and is paid per job instead of receiving employee wages or benefits.

ww.A full-time worker with benefits who tak: A full-time worker with benefits who takes orders from a boss is a regular employee, not an independent contractor.
ww.A manager at a company who hires and fir: A manager who hires and fires staff is part of the company as an employee and not an independent contractor.
ww.A person on probation at a new job in th: Someone on probation at a new job is still an employee, so this does not describe an independent contractor.

rw: Form 1099, commonly 1099-NEC, reports payments of $600 or more to independent contractors, who then report that income themselves.

ww.Form W-2 copy: A W-2 reports wages paid to employees, with taxes withheld, not payments made to independent contractors.
ww.Form W-4: Form W-4 tells an employer how much tax to withhold from an employee's pay, so it does not report payments to contractors.
ww.Form I-9: Form I-9 verifies a worker's identity and eligibility to work in the US, and does not report payments.

rw: With no tax withheld, a freelancer should set aside money and pay estimated quarterly taxes to avoid penalties and a big bill.

ww.Nothing, because freelance income is tax: Freelance income is taxable, including self-employment tax, even if no tax was withheld, so it is not tax free.
ww.Spend it all immediately on whatever you: Spending all of it ignores the tax bill that will come due, which could leave you owing money you do not have.
ww.Wait to see if the IRS asks you for any: Waiting for the IRS to ask can lead to penalties and interest, so freelancers should pay taxes without being asked.

rw: A benefit package is non-wage compensation, such as health insurance, retirement plans and paid leave, that adds to the value of a job.

ww.The hourly wage a worker earns, paid eve: An hourly wage is pay for work, whereas a benefit package is extra compensation beyond wages, such as insurance and leave.
ww.A schedule of shifts and breaks for the: A schedule of shifts and breaks is a work schedule and is not compensation, which is what a benefit package is.
ww.A fine for lateness that is taken from t: A fine for lateness would be a penalty or deduction, whereas a benefit package adds value to the worker's compensation.

rw: The employer match adds money to your 401(k) based on your own contributions, often a percentage up to a limit, which is free retirement money.

ww.A fee the employee pays to join the plan: The employer match is not a fee paid by the employee; it is money the employer adds to the account, so the claim is backward.
ww.A loan from the employer that is repaid: A match is a contribution made to your account by your employer, not a loan, and it does not require repayment with interest.
ww.A tax on the account that the worker pay: The match is not a tax on the account; it is an employer contribution that increases your retirement savings.

rw: You contribute 4% of $30,000 = $1,200, and a 100% match gives the employer's addition as $1,200.

ww.$12,000: $12,000 is 40% of salary and overstates the match; 4% of $30,000 is $1,200.
ww.$600: $600 is only 2% of salary, half of the correct match; the employer matches 100% of your 4%, which is $1,200.
ww.$120: $120 is only 0.4% of salary, a decimal error; 4% x $30,000 = $1,200 matched.

rw: A performance bonus is extra pay given for strong results, on top of regular wages, to reward and motivate employees.

ww.A tax on all earnings each year: A tax on earnings is a government charge on income, while a performance bonus is extra pay from an employer.
ww.A regular fixed wage each week: A regular fixed weekly wage is base pay, whereas a bonus is extra pay tied to results and not regular.
ww.A fine for very poor results: A fine for poor results would be a penalty, the opposite of a bonus, which rewards strong results.

rw: Commission is 4% x $30,000 = $1,200, and adding the $1,500 base gives total pay of $2,700.

ww.$31,500: $31,500 mistakes 4% for 105% or adds all sales to the base; commission is only 4% of $30,000, which is $1,200.
ww.$1,200: $1,200 is only the commission and leaves out the $1,500 base pay; total pay is $1,500 + $1,200 = $2,700.
ww.$3,000: $3,000 would need $1,500 in commission, about 5% of sales; 4% of $30,000 is $1,200, so total is $2,700.

rw: A gig economy job is short-term or freelance work, such as ridesharing or delivery, often arranged through an app, with flexible hours.

ww.A volunteer role at a charity or a local: Volunteer work is unpaid, whereas gig work is paid short-term or freelance work, so a charity role is not a gig job.
ww.A government role in a city office or a: A government job in a city office is typically a permanent public sector position, which is not what a gig is.
ww.A permanent salaried role with benefits: A permanent salaried role with benefits and a set schedule is traditional employment, the opposite of gig work.

rw: Income varies with the number of gigs available, and gig workers usually lack employer benefits like insurance and paid leave.

ww.Fixed schedules set by the employer for: Fixed schedules set by an employer are a feature of traditional jobs, whereas gig workers usually set their own hours.
ww.Guaranteed steady pay every week and mon: Guaranteed steady pay is not typical in gig work, where earnings depend on the jobs and demand, so it is not a downside.
ww.Employer-paid health insurance always at: Gig workers are usually independent contractors and typically must buy their own health insurance, so it is not paid at no cost.

rw: Minimum wage is the lowest hourly pay an employer may legally offer to covered workers, set by federal and state law.

ww.A bonus for new hires paid after one yea: A bonus for new hires is not minimum wage, which is a legal floor on hourly pay for all covered employees.
ww.The highest hourly pay allowed by law to: Minimum wage is a floor, not a ceiling; the law does not set the highest hourly pay allowed.
ww.The pay of managers and other executives: The pay of managers and executives is usually much higher and is not defined by minimum wage, which is a legal floor.

rw: When a state minimum wage is higher than the federal one, covered employers must pay the higher state rate because it gives workers more.

ww.Only the federal minimum wage: Following only the federal minimum would underpay workers where the state rate is higher; employers must meet the higher rate.
ww.Whichever of the two is lower: Following the lower wage would violate the higher standard; employers must follow whichever is higher.
ww.Neither of the two wages applies: Minimum wage laws do apply to covered employers, so saying neither applies is wrong; the higher one governs.

rw: Education builds skills and credentials that employers value, which tends to qualify workers for higher-paying jobs and raises earning potential.

ww.Education removes the need to work for a: Education does not remove the need to work; it raises skills and often pay, but people still work after earning degrees.
ww.Education lowers taxes on all of the inc: Education does not lower taxes on income; higher earnings can even raise taxes, but the benefit is higher earnings.
ww.Education guarantees a job without any e: Education improves job prospects but guarantees nothing; people must still apply, perform, and compete, so no job comes without effort.

rw: In-demand skills gained through training or education make workers more valuable to employers, which raises pay and improves job security over time.

ww.Working fewer hours with no goals, hopin: Working fewer hours with no goals and hoping for a job does not build skills or income, so it will not increase long-term earnings.
ww.Avoiding all training or classes that co: Avoiding training means skills fall behind demand, which limits job choices and pay, so it hurts long-term earnings.
ww.Changing jobs with no plan for what come: Changing jobs with no plan can cost income and experience, so it is not reliably going to improve long-term earnings.

rw: A budget starts by listing monthly income and expenses, so you know how much you have and where it goes before planning.

ww.Choosing what to buy, then adding up cos: Choosing purchases first and then adding costs is backward; a budget starts with what you have coming in and your regular expenses.
ww.Ignoring small purchases when you budget: Ignoring small purchases hides spending that adds up, such as coffee or snacks, so a budget should include them.
ww.Borrowing money to cover all your expens: Borrowing to cover expenses creates debt and does not begin a budget, which starts with knowing income and expenses.

rw: The 50/30/20 guideline allocates after-tax income as 50% to needs, 30% to wants, and 20% to savings and debt repayment.

ww.50% taxes, 30% wants and 20% gifts to fr: The 50/30/20 guideline is about needs, wants and savings, not taxes and gifts; this version does not match the rule.
ww.50% wants, 30% needs and 20% taxes paid: The rule gives 50% to needs and 30% to wants, so listing 50% wants and 30% needs swaps the categories.
ww.50% savings, 30% debt payments and 20% n: The rule gives 50% to needs, 30% to wants and 20% to savings and debt; this version puts savings first and does not fit.

rw: Wants get 30% of take-home pay, so $2,400 x 0.30 = $720 under the 50/30/20 guideline.

ww.$240: $240 is only 10% of $2,400, not the 30% wants share; 0.30 x $2,400 = $720.
ww.$480: $480 is 20% of $2,400, which is the savings and debt share, not wants; wants are 30%, or $720.
ww.$1,200: $1,200 is 50% of $2,400, which is the needs share; wants are 30%, which equals $720.

rw: A fixed expense stays the same amount each month, such as rent or a car payment, which makes it easy to plan for in a budget.

ww.A cost that is always zero every single: A cost that is always zero is not an expense at all; a fixed expense is a real cost that repeats at the same amount.
ww.A cost paid once in a lifetime, like a h: A one-time lifetime cost is a rare purchase, whereas a fixed expense recurs regularly at the same amount.
ww.A cost that changes every single month: A cost that changes every month is a variable expense, the opposite of a fixed expense that stays constant.

rw: A variable expense changes in amount from month to month, such as groceries, gas or entertainment, so budgets must estimate it.

ww.A cost that never changes at all in a ye: A cost that never changes is a fixed expense, such as rent, which is the opposite of a variable expense.
ww.A cost paid once at start-up of the busi: A start-up cost paid once is a one-time expense and not a variable expense, which recurs but changes in size.
ww.A cost that is the same every single mon: A cost that stays the same each month is a fixed expense, so it is the opposite of variable.

rw: Waiting 24 hours before non-essential purchases gives time for the urge to fade, so you buy only what you truly want.

ww.Shopping when you are bored or upset eac: Shopping when bored or upset makes impulse buying more likely, since emotions drive spending, so this habit increases it.
ww.Skipping the budget and spending at rand: Skipping the budget and spending at random removes limits and increases impulse buying, so it does not reduce it.
ww.Saving card numbers on every shopping si: Saving card numbers on shopping sites makes buying faster and easier, which increases impulse purchases.

rw: The 20 oz box costs $4.60 / 20 = $0.23 per ounce, less than the 12 oz box at $3.00 / 12 = $0.25, so it has the lower unit price.

ww.It cannot be determined from data: It can be determined: dividing price by ounces gives unit prices of $0.25 and $0.23, so the data are enough to compare.
ww.The 12 oz box at $0.25 per ounce: The 12 oz box costs $3.00 / 12 = $0.25 per ounce, which is higher than the 20 oz box, so it is not the lower unit price.
ww.They are exactly equal per ounce: The unit prices are not equal: $3.00 / 12 = $0.25 per ounce, while $4.60 / 20 = $0.23 per ounce.

rw: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative you give up, such as other uses for the same money.

ww.The shipping cost of the item that you b: Shipping is an extra monetary cost of an item, whereas opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative you give up.
ww.The price tag only, not what you give up: The price tag alone is the money cost; opportunity cost also counts what you give up, so a price-only answer omits it.
ww.The tax on the item you buy, added to th: Sales tax is a monetary cost added at checkout, not opportunity cost, which concerns forgone alternatives.

rw: Credit cards offer strong protection under federal law, which limits liability to $50 for unauthorized charges and lets you dispute charges.

ww.A wire transfer: Wire transfers are hard to reverse and offer little protection, and scammers often request them for that reason.
ww.A gift card: Gift cards are like cash and are difficult to recover if used in a scam, so they give little protection against unauthorized charges.
ww.Cash on delivery: Cash on delivery gives no way to dispute a charge after payment, so it offers little protection from unauthorized charges.

rw: Contacting the card issuer quickly lets you dispute the charge, and prompt reporting preserves your rights under consumer protection law.

ww.Ignore it and hope that the charge goes: Ignoring an unfamiliar charge lets fraud continue and may cost you the right to dispute it after the deadline passes.
ww.Cancel your internet service at once and: Cancelling internet service does not stop a card charge or fix the problem, since the issue lies with the card account.
ww.Pay it to avoid trouble, then ask for a: Paying a charge you never ordered can make it harder to recover your money; you should dispute it instead.

rw: Sales tax is a percentage added to the price of goods and some services at the point of purchase, collected by the seller for the state.

ww.A tax on property that you own, paid eac: A tax on property you own, paid each year, is a property tax; sales tax is paid at the point of sale.
ww.A tax on income that you earn, paid each: A tax on income earned is an income tax, which is paid on earnings, not added at checkout like sales tax.
ww.A tax on gifts that you get, paid each y: A tax on gifts received is a gift tax, which is different from sales tax charged at the register.

rw: Tax is $60 x 0.08 = $4.80, and adding it to the price gives $60 + $4.80 = $64.80.

ww.$68.00: $68.00 adds 8 dollars rather than 8 percent; the correct tax is $60 x 0.08 = $4.80, making the total $64.80.
ww.$60.80: $60.80 adds only 80 cents, treating 8% as 0.8%; the tax is $60 x 0.08 = $4.80, so the total is $64.80.
ww.$48.00: $48.00 subtracts 20% instead of adding tax; sales tax raises the price, so the total is $60 + $4.80 = $64.80.

rw: A need is something required to live, such as food, shelter, clothing and basic healthcare, which must be paid for before wants.

ww.Something advertised often on television: Something advertised often is a want driven by marketing and is not necessarily required for survival, so it is not a need.
ww.Something you would like but can live wi: Something you would like but can live without is a want, which is the opposite of a need.
ww.Something expensive that you buy for fun: An expensive item bought for fun on the weekend is a want and not required to live, so it is not a need.

rw: Buying groceries before a video game puts a need (food) ahead of a want (game), which is choosing needs over wants.

ww.Buying a game before paying the monthly: Buying a game before paying rent puts a want ahead of a need (housing), the reverse of the correct choice.
ww.Buying a concert ticket before medicine: Buying a concert ticket before medicine puts a want ahead of a need (health), the opposite of choosing needs first.
ww.Buying designer shoes instead of food: Buying designer shoes instead of food puts a want ahead of a need, so it is the opposite of choosing a need.

rw: A subscription is a recurring payment, such as monthly streaming, for ongoing access to a product or service until you cancel.

ww.A refund of the price paid for a product: A refund returns money after a purchase, whereas a subscription is a recurring payment for ongoing access to a service.
ww.A one-time purchase with no renewal, pai: A one-time purchase with no renewal is the opposite of a subscription, which renews and bills you repeatedly.
ww.A tax on services that a firm charges to: A tax on services is a government charge, which is a different concept from a subscription, which is a recurring payment.

rw: Three subscriptions at $10 each monthly cost $30 a month, and $30 x 12 months = $360 wasted yearly.

ww.$3,600: $3,600 is ten times too large; three subscriptions at $10 for 12 months is 3 x $10 x 12 = $360.
ww.$30: $30 is only one month of the three subscriptions; over 12 months it is $30 x 12 = $360.
ww.$120: $120 counts only one subscription for a year ($10 x 12); with three, the yearly waste is $360.

rw: Spending $340 on $300 of income is a $40 monthly shortfall, so the student should cut spending or raise income to avoid debt.

ww.Stop tracking spending and hope it works: Stopping tracking leaves the shortfall unexamined and likely leads to debt, so hoping it works out is not a plan.
ww.Borrow to keep spending the same and rep: Borrowing to keep spending the same adds debt and interest while the overspending problem remains, making it worse over time.
ww.Spend more to feel better about the shor: Spending more to feel better enlarges the $40 gap and deepens the shortfall, so it is the opposite of the fix.

rw: A coupon is a voucher that gives a discount on a purchase, either a set amount or a percentage off the price.

ww.A loan a store gives a shopper for a big: A loan a store gives for a large purchase is store financing, not a coupon, which is a voucher for a discount.
ww.A tax form a shopper fills out to report: A tax form for reporting purchases is not a coupon; a coupon is a voucher that lowers the price you pay.
ww.A warranty that promises to repair a pro: A warranty promises repair of a defective product, whereas a coupon gives a discount on a purchase.

rw: Store credit cards typically have high interest rates and offer a discount on store purchases, so carrying a balance can cost more than the savings.

ww.A lower rate than any bank card, as the: Store cards usually have higher rates than bank cards, not lower, and retailer backing does not make them cheaper.
ww.No repayment needed on the money that yo: Money spent on a store card must be repaid like any credit, so saying no repayment is needed is false.
ww.Protection from all fraud and identity t: A store card does not protect from all fraud; no card protects from every kind of fraud or identity theft.

rw: Saving prepares you for emergencies and future goals, such as a car or education, and reduces the need to borrow.

ww.It removes the need for a budget in your: Saving does not remove the need for a budget; a budget is how you plan to save and control spending.
ww.It guarantees you never need a job again: Saving does not guarantee you will never need a job; it helps cover costs but rarely replaces income forever.
ww.It makes you spend more money than you c: Saving means setting money aside, so it reduces spending rather than making you spend more than you earn.

rw: Emergency money belongs in a safe, easily accessible account, such as an insured savings account, so it is available quickly without loss.

ww.Under a mattress at home for safety: Under a mattress, cash can be stolen or destroyed, earns no interest, and is not protected by deposit insurance, so it is not a safe place.
ww.In a risky stock that could fall fast: A risky stock can fall fast just when you need cash, so it is unsuitable for emergency money.
ww.In a long-term account with penalties: A long-term account with penalties makes it costly to withdraw in an emergency, so it is not suited for emergency money.

rw: Year 1: $1,000 x 1.05 = $1,050. Year 2: $1,050 x 1.05 = $1,102.50, since interest earns interest.

ww.$1,200.00: $1,200.00 would require 10% growth per year; 5% simple growth for 2 years gives $1,100, and compounding gives $1,102.50.
ww.$1,050.00: $1,050.00 is the balance after only one year; a second year of interest brings the balance to $1,102.50.
ww.$1,100.00: $1,100 is simple interest ($50 each year); compounding adds interest on the first year's interest, giving $1,102.50.

rw: The Rule of 72 estimates how long money takes to double by dividing 72 by the annual interest rate.

ww.A rule setting retirement age, when work: The Rule of 72 has nothing to do with retirement age; it estimates how long it takes money to double.
ww.A rule for calculating taxes owed to the: The Rule of 72 is not a tax calculation; it divides 72 by the interest rate to estimate a doubling time.
ww.A rule for loan payments that lenders mu: The Rule of 72 is a mental math shortcut for savings growth and not a rule for loan payments that lenders follow.

rw: By the Rule of 72, doubling time is 72 / 6 = 12 years at a 6% annual interest rate.

ww.6 years: 6 years would require a 12% rate (72 / 12); at 6%, the Rule of 72 gives 72 / 6 = 12 years.
ww.8 years: 8 years would need a 9% rate (72 / 9 = 8); at 6% the doubling time is 72 / 6 = 12 years.
ww.72 years: 72 is the numerator of the rule and not the answer; dividing 72 by 6 gives 12 years to double.

rw: Account A compounds daily, so interest earns interest more often than in B, giving a slightly higher effective yield at the same 4% rate.

ww.Neither one: Compounding frequency matters; daily compounding adds interest more often, so one account does earn more than the other.
ww.About equal: The difference is small but real; daily compounding earns slightly more than annual compounding at the same 4% rate, so they are not equal.
ww.Account B: Annual compounding adds interest only once a year, so Account B earns slightly less than daily compounding at the same rate.

rw: A 529 plan is a tax-advantaged savings plan for education costs, with tax-free growth if used for qualified expenses like tuition.

ww.An insurance plan for cars and homes in: An insurance plan for cars and homes is not a 529; a 529 is a savings plan for education expenses.
ww.A retirement plan for company staff fund: A retirement plan funded by pay describes a 401(k), whereas a 529 plan is for education costs.
ww.A loan for homebuyers who put money down: A loan for homebuyers is a mortgage, which is borrowing, while a 529 is a savings plan, not a loan.

rw: With inflation at 3% and interest at 1%, prices rise faster than savings grow, so the real value, or buying power, of the savings decreases.

ww.It doubles: Real value does not double; with a 1% return below 3% inflation, buying power falls over time.
ww.It increases: Real value would increase only if interest exceeded inflation; here 1% is below 3%, so buying power falls.
ww.No change: There is a change because inflation outpaces the interest earned, shrinking the real purchasing power of the savings.

rw: Starting early gives compound interest more time to work, so earnings earn their own earnings and small deposits grow large.

ww.You can spend all of your income on fun: Spending all your income on fun does nothing for saving and does not explain why starting early helps.
ww.Banks pay young savers a much higher rat: Banks do not pay young savers a higher rate; the advantage of starting early comes from more time to compound.
ww.You never need to save again in your lif: Saving early does not mean you never need to save again; regular saving is still needed for years.

rw: Payment history is the largest factor in credit scores, and a payment 30 or more days late can sharply lower your score.

ww.Checking your own credit report yearly: Checking your own credit report is a soft inquiry and does not affect your score, so it cannot lower it.
ww.Keeping a card account open for years: Keeping a card open for years lengthens your credit history, which tends to help your score, not lower it.
ww.Paying the balance in full each month: Paying the balance in full each month shows responsible use and keeps utilization low, which helps your score.

rw: Keeping utilization below about 30 percent of your available credit shows responsible use, which supports a higher credit score.

ww.Exactly 100 percent at all times of the: Using 100 percent of your limit means being maxed out, which hurts your score and shows risk to lenders.
ww.More than your credit limit allows you t: Using more than your limit is not normally possible, and being near or over the limit is a negative for scores.
ww.Above 90 percent of the total available: Above 90 percent utilization signals heavy reliance on credit, which hurts your score; lower is better.

rw: Utilization is balance divided by limit: $1,000 / $4,000 = 0.25, which is 25%.

ww.400%: 400% flips the ratio ($4,000 / $1,000); utilization divides the balance by the limit, giving $1,000 / $4,000 = 25%.
ww.10%: 10% would need a $400 balance on a $4,000 limit; $1,000 / $4,000 is 25%.
ww.75%: 75% is the unused share of the limit ($3,000 / $4,000); the utilization rate is $1,000 / $4,000 = 25%.

rw: An installment loan is repaid in fixed regular payments over time, such as monthly payments on a car or student loan.

ww.A loan repaid in one lump sum at the len: A loan repaid in one lump sum at the lender's choice is not an installment loan, which has set scheduled payments.
ww.A gift that never needs any repayment at: A gift never needs repayment, whereas an installment loan must be repaid in regular payments plus interest.
ww.A credit line with no end date at all fo: A credit line with no end date is revolving credit, which differs from an installment loan with a set term.

rw: Revolving credit lets you borrow up to a limit, repay it, and borrow again, as with credit cards.

ww.A loan repaid in fixed payments over set: A loan repaid in fixed payments over set months is an installment loan, not revolving credit.
ww.A loan with no interest that you never r: A loan with no interest that you never repay does not exist; revolving credit must be repaid and usually charges interest.
ww.A one-time cash gift from a bank to a cu: A cash gift from a bank is not credit; revolving credit is borrowed money that you must repay.

rw: A 48-month car loan is repaid in fixed monthly installments over a set term, making it a classic installment loan.

ww.A home equity loan line: A home equity line of credit is revolving credit, which you can borrow and repay again, unlike an installment loan.
ww.A store credit card: A store credit card is revolving credit, with a limit you can use repeatedly, not a fixed-payment installment loan.
ww.A bank credit card: A bank credit card is revolving credit, so it is not installment credit.

rw: A loan origination fee is a charge by the lender for processing and setting up a new loan, often a percentage of the loan.

ww.A fee for using an ATM machine abroad: An ATM fee for use abroad is a foreign bank charge, unrelated to the cost of setting up a new loan.
ww.A fee charged for paying off early: A fee for paying off early is a prepayment penalty, not an origination fee, which is charged when the loan begins.
ww.A fee for paying a bill very late: A fee for paying a bill late is a late fee and not an origination fee, which is charged to open the loan.

rw: A prepayment penalty is a fee some lenders charge for paying off a loan early, because they lose expected interest income.

ww.A tax on loan interest that borrowers pa: A tax on loan interest is a government charge and has nothing to do with the lender's prepayment penalty.
ww.A fee for paying late on a loan or a cre: A fee for paying late is a late fee; a prepayment penalty is charged for paying the loan off early.
ww.A reward for paying early on a loan from: A reward for paying early is the opposite of a penalty; a prepayment penalty is a cost for early payoff, not a prize.

rw: Checking fees, the interest rate and prepayment terms before signing reveals the true cost and helps you avoid surprise charges later.

ww.The size of the lender's main building: The size of the lender's building tells you nothing about the cost; fees, rate and terms determine the total price.
ww.The color of the loan paperwork forms: The color of the paperwork has no effect on cost, so it does not help you avoid surprises.
ww.The name of the loan officer who helps y: The loan officer's name does not affect the cost of the loan; the terms in the contract do.

rw: The total cost of a loan is the principal plus all interest and fees, so it shows what you actually pay to borrow.

ww.The monthly payment only, times the mont: The monthly payment times months gives total payments, but this leaves out fees, so it is not the full cost of the loan.
ww.The interest rate only, with no fees inc: The interest rate alone does not include fees or principal, so it is not the total cost of a loan.
ww.The principal only, with no interest or: The principal is only the amount borrowed and leaves out the interest and fees that make borrowing cost more.

rw: The cost of borrowing is total repaid minus amount borrowed: $5,800 - $5,000 = $800, which is the interest and fees.

ww.$5,800: $5,800 is the total repaid and includes the $5,000 borrowed; the cost of borrowing is $5,800 - $5,000 = $800.
ww.$10,800: $10,800 adds the borrowed amount to the repayment; the cost of borrowing is only the extra paid, $800.
ww.$5,000: $5,000 is the amount borrowed and not the cost; the extra paid beyond it is $5,800 - $5,000 = $800.

rw: A down payment is an upfront payment toward a purchase that reduces the amount you must borrow and can lower interest cost.

ww.A monthly loan payment that you make to: A monthly loan payment is an installment, not a down payment, which is paid upfront at the start.
ww.A fee for paying late on a loan or a cre: A fee for paying late is a late fee, not a down payment, which is paid at purchase to reduce the loan.
ww.A refund the seller pays back to the buy: A refund from the seller to the buyer is not a down payment, which is a buyer's upfront payment.
